This
document covers the sewage water treatment plant of Ayoun
Moussa PS.

The
system collects sewage water from power station in various sumps for treatment.
Sewage water is treated, then discharged back to the Red Sea via the seal well
in the circulating water discharge.

Sewage
treatment plant properties will comply with the requirement of
Egyptian Law number (4) for year 1994.

This
document initiated by chemist: Mohamed Elshahat Abd Elmonem and Reviewed by eng:
Nageh Elsaman Ahmed, control by quality chemist: Saad sadeek at EDEPC,
and approved by eng: Mahmoud Elnakeeb; head sector of operation and accepted by
eng: Tarek Youssef Aly head sector of Ayoun Moussa Power Station.

The sewage water is drained to the sanitary water lift
stations by gravity mains. The water is accumulated in the lift stations; when
the water reaches a predetermined level, the lift station pumps start pumping
the water out of the lift station and to the sewage treatment plant.

There are five sanitary water lift stations on site, apart from the colony 
sewage system. Each lift station contains two pumps; one in operation mode and 
the other in standby mode.

The pump system including the pump, motor, and power cable
is approved for use in areas classified as hazardous locations, in accordance
with the NEC Class1, Division1, Group C and D. As required by Factory
Manual, the motor shall be capable of operating in pumped media up to 400ºC. The motor thermal switch shall allow
safe motor operation up to 1270ºC.
In addition, an internal flat switch shall be available in the motor chamber.

Equipment is
designed to have a life of not less than 30 years at specified conditions
excluding expendable items such as packing, seals & gaskets.

Each lift
station contains two submersible, non-clog, and wastewater pumps per lift
station. Each pump is equipped with submersible, electric motor, rated
for 400 V, 3 phase, 50 HZ operation. The pumps are supplied with a mating cast
iron discharge connections and shall be capable of delivering the required
flow, at the total dynamic head.

The pumps are
firmly connected to the discharge connection, guided by not less than two guide
bars extending from the top of the station to discharge connection.

The incoming
raw sewage is delivered to the plant Aeration Zone via an inlet box and inlet
bar screen and passes through communitor. In the Aeration Zone the raw effluent
is mixed with returned activated sludge from the Settling Zone and continuously
aerated with air from the plant air blowers. This air supplies the oxygen
necessary for growth of the micro-organisms and also ensures that the returned
activated sludge and incoming raw sewage are thoroughly mixed. After a
retention period in the aeration compartment (approx. 48 hours), the treated
liquor passes through a transfer pipe into the Settling Zone.

The Settling
Zone allows the sludge and supernatant to separate. The supernatant liquor
overflows an annular V notched weir into a collecting channel and hence into
the chlorine contact tank. The sludge settles and accumulates in the Settling
Zone where it is continuously withdrawn by two ( service/ standby submersible pumps) and returned
to the Aeration Zone. Excess sludge that builds up in the system is
periodically wasted through a manually operated valve.

Three air
blowers are provided ( two in operation and one standby). Each blower is
controlled with an On/Off switch on the control panel. A timer is provided in
the control circuit for automatic operation.

Air from the
air blowers is admitted to the Aeration Zone via a number of air diffusers
situated in the bottom of the Aeration Zone.

Sodium
hypochlorite solution is dosed into the treated effluent tank in order to
disinfect the treated effluent.

The sodium hypochlorite dosing set is located
in the blower house with the dosing pumps ON/OFF switch located on the control
panel.
The basic equation for dosing is:
INITIAL DOSAGE in mg/l = DEMAND in mg/l + RESIDUAL in mg/l

The amount of 
chlorine required to disinfect the treated water will vary according to the 
composition of the sewage and the degree of disinfection to be achieved, and 
usually vary between 4 to 12 mg/l in order to maintain a satisfactory chlorine 
residual of 0.5 to 1.0 mg/l.

The treated 
effluent out from the settling tank flows by gravity into the treated effluent 
storage tank.

This tank is 
designed with baffle walls to ensure sufficient time for chlorine dispersal 
before the treated effluent is withdrawn through pumps.

Two pumps are
provided to feed the irrigation network. They are equipped the required suction
and delivery isolating valves and a non return valve for each unit.

Drying beds,
are provided to receive and drain water from the excess activated sludge. This
group is provided with an integral Supernatant Tank. The drained water is
collected in this tank and returned to the aeration tank.

In the extended aeration treatment plant the incoming raw sewage containing the organic
matter, is mixed with previously aerated sewage that is rich in micro-organisms
and referred to as activated sludge.

The mixture of activated sludge and raw sewage is aerated to
provide the oxygen necessary for the biological degradation of the organic
matter, and to assist in the mixing process. The air must be continuously 
supplied.

As long as the bacterial colony in the 
treatment plant is well aerated and healthy, there will be no odors from 
treatment process.

After aeration the mixed liquor is passed to a 
Settling Zone
to allow the activated sludge to settle out prior to recycling, and to allow
the supernatant liquor to overflow a weir board to the chlorine contact tank.
The excess activated sludge that builds up in the Settling Zone is periodically
discharged to sludge drying beds for disposal. After that the treated effluent
is disinfected with chlorine to destroy harmful micro-organisms. The chlorine
is dosed in the outgoing pipe to the treated effluent tank to provide a 0.5
mg/l residual chlorine in the Treated Effluent Tank.

After preliminary
and biological treatment, the water parameters must completely with the
following standards:

One set of fittings for
reinforced concrete chamber. Chamber dimension 5.0 x 1.0 x 0.8m depth.

One
set of fitting for the mild steel chamber. Chamber dimension 3.5 x 0.9 x 0.6m
depth.

Tank
dimension: 6.5 M x
8 M x 4M depth

Confirm that the plant has been installed according to 
instructions manual and it is filled with water or sewage.
Check the sewage pumps and their float switches.
Check that blower gear case oil level is correct.

Check that the 
chemical dosing pumps are working.

Start the
blowers and make sure that the blowing of air is sufficient in the aerated
section of the grease trap, balancing, selector, aeration tank and sludge
holding tank. Allow the blowers to run continuously and check the plant
daily. Foaming will almost certainly occur for few days if activated
sludge is not seed.

After one
week, the mixed liquor in the Aeration Zone should become brown in color and
settle rapidly when a sample is examined in a jar test, using the 30
minutes settlement test explained later. If the mixed liquor has an odor, 
the Air Supply should be increased.

After three
weeks, the plant should be producing a good clear effluent with no smell, apart
from a faint earthly odor similar to damp soil. In cases where the
initial load on the plant is much less than that of the design load, the
results may take longer to attain.

Start the
recycling airlifts at approximately 2/3 of their maximum output by opening the
gate valve and closing gate valve.

Do not start
the excess sludge removal as long as a sufficient concentration (300 ml) of
activated sludge is maintained in the aeration tank.

To maintain 
the plant at a good operating conditions, a daily routine sludge settling test 
should take place and desludging is done at 20-40 % ratio.

Foaming may 
require from time to time and is generally an indication that too much activated 
sludge has been removed. Adjust the sludge removal routine as necessary.

Don't adjust 
the stroke length when the pump is stationary; adjustment must only be made 
during suction stroke.

To disinfect 
the treated effluent, start the pump and set it at approximately half stroke and 
after 15 minutes contact time, measure the chlorine content in the contact tank 
and then adjust the pump output to maintain 0.5 mg/l residual chlorine. Repeat 
chlorine tests at regular intervals, and adjust the pump delivery accordingly.

Once the plant is in normal 
operation, the following conditions should be maintained.

Optimum percentage of settled
 sludge to be established from operating experience.

Sparkling clear
 appearance with a residual chlorine content of 0.5 mg\l
